The Amusement Park Pricing Puzzle

Sell the same ride three ways: per ride, a flat pass, and a two-part tariff. Per-ride pricing charges like a monopolist and cuts use. A flat pass makes extra rides free, so guests overuse them. A two-part tariff splits the bill into an entry fee and a per-ride price. Price rides at cost and collect the leftover gain at the gate, and the waste vanishes. The payment formula is below. For example, running one ride costs the park 500 won. At 3,000 won a ride, 🧑 kids ride only twice. A 5,000-won entry fee plus 500 won a ride makes five rides feel fine. The park pockets its gain in the entry fee.

payment=F+pq\text{payment} = F + pqpayment=F+pq
F=consumer surplus at p=MCF = \text{consumer surplus at } p = MCF=consumer surplus at p=MC

Examples & Exercises

Rides at an amusement park face demand q=14−Pq = 14 - Pq=14−P and cost 222 per ride. With a two-part tariff that sets the per-ride price equal to cost, p=2p = 2p=2, and charges only an entry fee, how many rides does a guest take, and what is the most the park can charge at the gate?

Show proof
  1. With the per-ride price equal to cost, the guest rides until one more ride is worth exactly 222: q=14−2=12q = 14 - 2 = 12q=14−2=12 rides.
  2. Over those 121212 rides the guest holds surplus of the triangle (14−2)×122=72\frac{(14 - 2) \times 12}{2} = 722(14−2)×12​=72. Set the entry fee to exactly 727272 and the guest still (just barely) walks in, while the park's profit is 727272 — with zero waste.
  3. By comparison, per-ride pricing alone gives the monopoly price p=8p = 8p=8, only 666 rides, profit 363636, and deadweight loss 181818. The two-part tariff bakes the whole cake — and takes it all.

The same guest (q=14−Pq = 14 - Pq=14−P, cost 222 per plate) goes to a buffet. A flat 989898 makes every extra plate free. How many plates do they eat, and how much is wasted for society as a whole?

Show proof
  1. With a marginal price of 000, the guest eats until a plate is worth nothing: q=14−0=14q = 14 - 0 = 14q=14−0=14 plates.
  2. But plates beyond 121212 are worth less than their cost of 222. The waste is the small triangle over that stretch, 2×22=2\frac{2 \times 2}{2} = 222×2​=2. Total welfare is 98−2×14=7098 - 2 \times 14 = 7098−2×14=70 — exactly 222 short of the efficient 727272.
  3. Charging just 222 per plate would have stopped the guest at 121212 and erased the waste. The buffet's convenience is bought with those last plates.
